title: Preseason Poll Roundup: Where Michigan Football lands heading into Week 1
description: With preseason polls being released left and right, we take a look across the landscape to see where Michigan Football falls:
fullText:
With Week 1 of the college football season just a couple weeks away, several outlets have begun publishing their preseason rankings. While preseason polls in and of themselves are silly — as no snaps of football have been played on the field yet — they can be a good way to judge how the national media perceives your program.

With that in mind, we compiled a few of the notable polls and projections to paint a picture of how the media views Kyle Whittingham's program heading into the 2026 season.

In the first AP Poll of the year, the Wolverines sit at No. 16 in the country.

Ranked 16th in the Preseason AP Poll pic.twitter.com/sjg8Hypths

Sadly, the AP has Ohio State at No. 1 and Oregon at No. 2. Other notable Big Ten teams to make the top-25 include No. 6 Indiana, No. 14 USC, No. 17 Washington, No. 18 Penn State and No. 22 Iowa. Illinois and Minnesota also received votes.

The coaches agree with the media, as they also have the Wolverines at No. 16. The two sources are shockingly similar with just a handful of differences between the two in the top-16 teams. The coaches have Texas (4) ahead of Notre Dame (5) while the AP has them flipped. Similarly, the coaches have Oklahoma at No. 9 and Ole Miss at No. 10, while the AP has the inverse.

As for Big Ten representation, all the same teams appear in each poll in roughly the same landing spot. Nebraska did receive some votes from the coaches.

CBS Sports has Michigan one spot higher than the AP and coaches polls, with BYU being the team the Wolverines jumped. Whittingham aught to love that. The rest of the rankings are nearly a mirror image to that of the two polls above.

CBS is also slightly down on the SEC. CBS has Georgia at No. 5, while the other polls primarily have them at No. 3. They also have Texas A&M down at No. 11 while the AP has it at No. 8.

Love him or hate him, Josh Pate is an ascending voice in the college football media landscape. Pate's preseason model has the Wolverines at 15th in the country. Notably, he has Georgia at No. 2, much higher than everyone else. He also has BYU down at No. 19, a bit lower than the other polls in this article.

As for the rest of the Big Ten, Pate has Ohio State at 1, Oregon at 3, Indiana at 5, USC at 13, Penn State at 21, Illinois at 23 and Washington at 25.

If this roundup has taught you anything, it should be that preseason polls tend to mirror each other because we don't really know what these teams will look like on the field yet. Expect rapid reshuffling once the season gets going.

fullText:
LUSAKA, Zambia (AP) — Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was declared the winner Tuesday of a troubled election that saw vote counting suspended at one point because of violence at polling stations and opposition officials arrested during a law enforcement raid in which gunshots were fired.

Hichilema secured around 60% of the presidential vote in the southern African nation that has held largely peaceful elections since it returned to multiparty democracy in 1991.

Hichilema's main challenger, opposition leader Brian Mundubile, won around 38% of the vote, according to the electoral commission.

Zambia, a nation of 22 million people that is one of the world's leading copper producers, is a focus for Chinese investment because of its reserves of the critical mineral. It has also drawn interest from the United States under a Trump administration plan to increase U.S. access to copper and other critical minerals used in new technologies and renewable energy systems.

The results released early Tuesday followed days of heightened tensions since last Thursday's election.

The electoral commission suspended vote counting for hours on Friday, citing attacks on some polling station officials and what it called the theft of some ballot boxes.

It didn't say who might be responsible for the alleged violence and theft, but the suspension prompted the deployment of the army to parts of the capital, Lusaka — an unusual development for one of Africa's more stable democracies.

The Zambian government announced later that 11 opposition officials were detained in a law enforcement raid on election night at a property where opposition leader Mundubile was present, though he was not arrested, according to the government.

The raid involved an exchange of gunfire between occupants of the premises and law enforcement officers, the government said.

The government accused the opposition officials of being in possession of "high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection" and said they were a national security threat.

Mundubile criticized the raid as an attempt on his life and denied allegations that the officials were part of a militia.

Hichilema said in a statement Tuesday that he and his party were humbled by the trust placed in them by voters and also reached out to opposition supporters.

"To those citizens who preferred the ideas presented by our opponents, we hear you, and we will continue to work for you to ensure that every Zambian benefits from the development we are delivering," Hichilema said.

A preliminary report by a European Union observer team released before results were announced said the election was largely peaceful but the "broader electoral process took place in an environment that limited fundamental freedoms."

"Late legal changes, legal uncertainty and unequal campaign conditions distorted the playing field," said Michael McNamara, chief of the EU observer mission.

The 64-year-old Hichilema's campaign for a second term focused on an economic recovery plan for a country that was mired in a debt crisis when it defaulted on repayments in 2020. Hichilema was first elected in 2021, and Zambia has restructured debt payments, reined in inflation and stabilized its currency under his leadership.

One of Hichilema's main pledges has been to more than triple Zambia's copper production to 3 million tons a year by the end of his final term in 2031.

Critics, however, said the effects of those macroeconomic improvements were not being felt by ordinary Zambians who were growing frustrated with a high cost of living and electricity shortages.

Hichilema vowed "meaningful development for every single Zambian, in every corner of our country."

Magome reported from Johannesburg.

Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Monday pushed for a change in American elections, advocating for more competition.

He cited the 2024 election, remarking to NewsNation's Elizabeth Vargas, "all we ever heard reported about was the seven battleground states."

"Forty-three were predetermined. Four hundred and thirty-five congressional districts in the United States of America, 395 are predetermined, already predetermined. Something's wrong. There's no competition," he continued.

Manchin argued for open primaries with more candidates.

"Open the primaries up, let people run in the primaries, and basically, then, take your top four or five, go to the general election, and make sure that when you get elected, you get elected by a majority, not plurality, just a majority, 50 plus one. Then you start having more of a representative form of government."

Last month, Manchin, a former Democrat, announced a new organization with a goal of recruiting and electing independent candidates to Congress.

Manchin launched the Independent Leadership Council (ILC), which is centered on building support and infrastructure for candidates not running in the two mainstream American parties in congressional races. He leads the organization with his daughter, Heather Bresch.

"We're not trying to start another party," the former senator said in an interview with CNN. "We're trying to get a person who can be committed to — and totally committed to — being an independent with an independent voice. They can vote with Democrats and Republicans when they're right and speak out against them when they're wrong."

Manchin told CNN previously that he was not looking to run for office again and that he wanted to assist in electing candidates willing to work with both sides of the aisle.

"I don't see me getting back into the fray, I really don't," he said. "Now I'm trying to help people around the country that want that same outcome."

"DHS will always fight to protect the integrity of our elections, because election security is national security. Only Americans should be electing American leaders," he continued.

title: Who is Byron Donalds? The Trump ally is favored to become Florida's next governor.
description: It’s been over three decades since the Sunshine State elected a Democratic governor, but polls suggest the MAGA favorite could be in for a tight race in November.
fullText:
In February 2025, President Trump made a surprising endorsement in the Florida governor's race. It wasn't who he chose, but when he decided to back them that was unexpected. The primary was still 18 months away and the man he endorsed hadn't even declared his candidacy yet.

Still, Trump's word carries so much weight in the Republican Party, particularly in his newly adopted home state, that Rep. Byron Donalds quickly became the frontrunner in the Florida GOP gubernatorial primary.

"Byron Donalds would be a truly Great and Powerful Governor for Florida and, should he decide to run, will have my Complete and Total Endorsement," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time. "RUN, BYRON, RUN!"

Donalds formally entered the race five days after Trump's post. Throughout his campaign, polls have shown him well ahead of the other Republican candidates. If he wins the GOP primary on Tuesday, he would also be the favorite to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, who is ineligible to run for a third term.

It has been more than three decades since Florida elected a Democrat as its governor, but some of the GOP's victories during that span have been extremely close. Republicans are counting on Donalds to keep their winning streak alive as he gears up for what polls suggest could be another close contest against likely Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who left the GOP during Trump's first presidential term.

Here's a guide to who Byron Donalds is, what he stands for and what his potential election might mean for America's third most populous state.

Donalds, 47, was born in New York City in 1978. He is of Jamaican and Panamanian heritage and was raised by his mother, describing himself as the "product of a single-parent household." Donalds grew up in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn before moving to Florida for college. He graduated from Florida State University in 2002 with a bachelor's degree in finance and marketing, and stayed in Florida to launch a career in the banking and insurance industries.

Donalds has said that his inspiration to go into politics came from anger over how Congress handled the aftermath of the 2008 financial collapse and the ensuing bank bailouts. A registered Democrat at the time, Donalds opted to switch parties and embraced the fiscally conservative worldview of the burgeoning tea party movement, which advocated for low taxes and reduced government spending.

"I got mad," Donalds said during a podcast interview earlier this month. "It pissed me off. That's how I got into politics and from there got involved in the Tea Party."

As a young Black man, Donalds stood out within a movement that was largely associated with older white voters. In 2012, he joined a crowded GOP primary for an open House seat, but finished fifth out of six candidates. In 2016, he was elected to the Florida state legislature.

He ran for Congress again in 2020 and, after being labeled a "Rising Star" by Trump following his primary win, was elected to the House of Representatives for the first time. He was the third Black Republican in history to represent Florida on Capitol Hill.

When he joined Congress, Donalds was part of a group of conservative lawmakers called the "Freedom Force," who were dedicated to countering the influence of progressive lawmakers like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. One of his first acts after being sworn in was to challenge the certification of the 2020 presidential election. He has repeatedly said that he does not believe that Joe Biden was a legitimately elected president.

In 2023, his name was raised as a potential House speaker multiple times during a drawn-out leadership crisis that ultimately led to Rep. Mike Johnson being elected speaker.

Donalds has been married to his wife, Erika Lees, since 2003. They have three children together. According to Donalds's first wife, Bisa Hall, Donalds began dating Lees while he and Hall were still married. Hall told WGCU News their marriage was not romantic and that they only wed to resolve what she described as a "residency issue" affecting her ability to attend college in Florida.

In 2022, Donalds was captured on camera having a heated argument with a woman inside a supermarket in Naples, Fla. The woman, Kelly Mason, who is currently a member of the Collier County School Board, filed a civil lawsuit over the incident in July, accusing him of assault. In a statement, Donalds's campaign called the lawsuit "baseless" and "politically motivated."

Donalds has closely aligned himself with Trump's MAGA policies. The words "Enact the Trump Agenda" appear in large bold letters at the top of the "issues" page of his campaign website.

He has endorsed Trump's sweeping immigration crackdown, including arguing that undocumented immigrants facing deportation should not be entitled to due process under the law and criticizing the Supreme Court for striking down the president's attempt to revoke birthright citizenship.

Donalds is staunchly conservative on social issues. He supports placing strict limits on abortion access, wants to expand gun rights, has called for eliminating "woke ideology" in schools and supports restrictions on transgender rights, including barring transgender women and girls from women's sports. Donalds has also said he does not believe in man-made climate change.

If elected, he has pledged to block "sanctuary" jurisdictions that don't comply with federal immigration enforcement from receiving state funding, give parents more influence over their children's education and reform Florida's struggling property insurance industry.

The last time Florida elected a new governor with Trump in the White House was in the "blue wave" midterm cycle of 2018, when DeSantis narrowly defeated Democrat Andrew Gillum by less than half a percentage point. Though the national political environment appears to be swinging against the GOP again this year, polls have shown Donalds holding a steady lead of roughly five percentage points in head-to-head general election matchups.

title: Scottish FA withdraws support for Fifa president Infantino
description: The Scottish Football Association has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino and will not be voting for his re-election as president of Fifa, chief executive Ian Maxwell has told BBC Sport.
fullText:
The Scottish Football Association has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino and will not be voting for his re-election as president of Fifa, chief executive Ian Maxwell has told BBC Sport.

It comes as FairSquare, a non-profit organisation which campaigns for accountability in sport, wrote to Fifa's governance, audit and compliance committee requesting that Infantino be ruled ineligible to run again for the presidency.

Infantino is under increasing pressure over his attempt, later abandoned, to create a new company to manage the commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including the World Cups, with 21% to be sold off to a private investment company.

Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) was aborted after widespread criticism from several confederations, led by Uefa, which has threatened a boycott of all Fifa competitions.

"The position of the SFA has been clear since the 55 Uefa associations met," said Maxwell, speaking as he announced Belgian Sebastian Pocognoli as the new Scotland head coach.

"We have aligned ourselves with the Uefa position and 55 nations are stronger than one voice.

"Their statement since then has talked about a lack of confidence in the Fifa leadership and the Scottish FA agree completely with that decision.

"The SFA will not be voting for Gianni Infantino come the re-election in early 2027."

Maxwell rejected the suggestion that the SFA had previously failed to publicly state it no longer supported Infantino because its president, Mike Mulraney, heads up the Fifa finance committee.

The Football Associations of England, Wales and the Republic of Ireland have already declared they have withdrawn support for Infantino, who is scheduled to stand for a fourth term as president in March.

FairSquare has called into question Infantino's right to stand for re-election "on the basis that he is already serving his third and final term".

Fifa statutes state that a president can only serve three terms of four years for a maximum of 12 years. Next year Infantino is hoping to win a fourth which, by 2031, would stretch his tenure to 15 years.

It stems from the Swiss-Italian replacing Sepp Blatter in 2016 and effectively serving the remainder of that term, which ended in 2019. Infantino was re-elected that year, and again in 2023.

In 2022, Infantino managed to successfully argue his case to the governance, audit and compliance committee that the 2016-2019 term should be discounted as it was not four years, making him eligible to stand in 2027.

But FairSquare argues that Infantino being president for 15 years clearly breaks the purpose of the regulation.

In the letter seen by BBC Sport, FairSquare says the decision "clearly violates the letter and purpose of the Fifa statutory provision on presidential term limits".

Written to the three members of the Fifa review committee, it adds that "such an exception has been made without a clear legal basis, in a non-transparent manner and without any reasoning to support it".

It questions the role of the Fifa Council in granting the exemption, rather than it being a decision of the Fifa Congress. It also questions why no written justification has ever been published.

Last week, Fifa and Infantino were accused of breaking trust "through deception", in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.

The letter, signed by the presidents and general secretaries of the three regional governing bodies, said recent controversy over the FFE proposal was fundamentally about "the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it".

While the statement did not name Infantino, sources have told BBC Sport that it should be seen as an opportunity for him to resign and leave his position with dignity.

Fifa has committed to presenting a report on FFE to the next meeting of the Fifa council, which is expected to take place in October.

The three confederations said this failed to "recognise that proper governance in the face of such a profound lack of judgement would require that such a review be conducted by a fully independent third party".

It also underlined a legal warning made by Uefa that Fifa should not delete or destroy any documents related to the abandoned plans.

BBC Sport understands that there have been preliminary discussions between the three confederations over breakaway competitions, should Infantino remain in situ. However, substantive talks are yet to begin, according to others.

At present there is no candidate who has put their name forward to stand against Infantino, before a 18 November deadline.

The football world appears to have been split down the middle by the issue, with the confederations of Africa, South America and Oceania having backed Infantino.

But even within confederations there is disagreement and it makes it very difficult to predict whether Infantino or his opponents have the upper hand in this battle.

In Oceania, which has 11 member associations, New Zealand has said it will not follow the confederation and vote for him.

Mexico, Grenada and St Kitts and Nevis have broken away from the other 32 Concacaf nations to support the Fifa president.

Of the 46 Asian confederations members, so far eight countries have split to champion Infantino's cause - the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Kuwait, Mongolia, the Philippines and Bhutan.

The Fifa Council, on which there are 36 confederation and national association heads plus Infantino, seems similarly split.

It raises questions about whether Infantino has the political power to govern Fifa, even if he wins an election of the 211 member associations.

The first test of Uefa's threat is just over three weeks away, when the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup is set to kick off. It is being hosted by Poland and features five other European nations, including England.

title: Republicans won the redistricting competition. Don't tell that to this California congressman
description: One thing Anne Smull, a retired feedstore owner, was looking forward to on Election Day was voting for the man who currently represents her in Congress, conservative Rep. Kevin Kiley.  During a recent...
fullText:
LINCOLN, Calif. (AP) — One thing Anne Smull, a retired feedstore owner, was looking forward to on Election Day was voting for the man who currently represents her in Congress, conservative Rep. Kevin Kiley. Now she can't.

That's because California Democrats sliced Kiley's district six ways as payback for Republican redistricting in Texas and elsewhere. The chunk of the district that Smull, who identifies as a conservative, lives in is now grafted onto an overwhelmingly Democratic seat based in the state's wine country.

During a recent lunch at a cafe in Lincoln, a onetime agricultural town that has morphed into a bedroom community on the edge of Sacramento's exurban sprawl, Smull was heartbroken to hear she can no longer vote for Kiley.

"He believes in the same things I do," Smull said. "It feels sneaky and underhanded."

Democratic voters in several other states know how Smull feels.

President Donald Trump last year told GOP-controlled states to redraw their maps before this year's midterm elections to increase the number of winnable seats for Republicans in order to help the party hold onto the U.S. House. The effort was turbocharged by a U.S. Supreme Court decision this spring that neutralized a key provision of the Voting Rights Act and cleared the way for Republicans to redraw more seats across the South that had elected Black Democrats.

Democratic-leaning and heavily minority communities from Texas to Tennessee have been split into multiple congressional districts that dilute the Democratic vote by stretching deep into conservative areas.

In the future, it is likely that more Republican voters in other states will go through what Smull and other conservatives in Northern California are facing. Democrats in Maryland, New York, Illinois and other strongholds have pledged to retaliate in time for the 2028 elections and split Republican-leaning districts the way their California counterparts did Kiley's.

Democrats have been hindered nationally by stricter rules against partisan line-drawing in their states, but California showed a way around that. California Democrats won voter approval last year to redraw the state's congressional map, originally made by an independent commission, and formed five new Democratic-leaning seats.

Kiley's is one of them. The reworked political lines led the two-term congressman to leave the Republican Party and run as an independent in the slightly Democratic-leaning district that now includes his home.

He spoke out against partisan gerrymandering, even unsuccessfully trying to force the Republican-led House to allow a vote on a bill to ban mid-decade redistricting.

"We've seen partisan divisions really spin out of control in really harmful ways, and I think exhibit number one is the redistricting wars," Kiley recently told a group of voters in the suburb of Citrus Heights.

Democrats contend Kiley's party switch is purely a political trick to survive in a more liberal district. They note he still caucuses with House Republicans, has voted for many of the GOP's priorities, including Trump's sweeping budget and tax cut bill last year, and that political organizations run by House Republicans are spending money to back his reelection.

Even some of Kiley's supporters think the election was a factor in the congressman's decision to become an independent.

"My original thinking was he did it because of redistricting — maybe it'd help him get reelected," said John Coburn, a 68-year-old retired business owner, at the Citrus Heights event.

Coburn is furious at the Democrats' redistricting and hopes Kiley wins. Coburn does not care that they did it in retaliation for Texas, where Republicans at Trump's directive revised that state's map to carve out up to five new winnable conservative seats.

"I don't care about Texas, I live in California," Coburn said, adding that "40% of the state is Republican, and we have zero voice. Zero. It's not how our Founding Fathers intended."

In an interview, Kiley said his switch to independent was no political gambit. If he wanted to stay in the House, he argued, he could have had an easier time staying in the GOP, moving to a more conservative district that included parts of his old one and running in a Republican primary there.

"I could have gone there and run and played the same game these other politicians are playing," he said.

Kiley said he is caucusing with Republicans to avoid losing his seats on committees and that in the next Congress he will try to change rules so independent members do not lose committee seats because they do not caucus with one of the two major parties.

Among his backers, he noted, is onetime Democratic presidential hopeful Andrew Yang, a former technology entrepreneur who co-founded a centrist party for independents.

The Democrat running against Kiley, former state Sen. Richard Pan, scoffs at his rival's newfound independent status.

"He was a MAGA champion when he first ran for Congress, and now he's trying to say 'I'm not,'" Pan told a crowd at a senior community in Roseville, referring to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.

Earlier that day, Pan swung by the Placer County Democratic Party office, tucked away on the second story of a brick shopping arcade in Lincoln's compact downtown.

Placer is a Republican county that stretches from the Sacramento suburbs to the northwestern shores of Lake Tahoe. The entire county is in Kiley's current district, but it will be divided among three districts in the new map.

Kathleen Crawford, chair of the county Democratic Party, was enthusiastic about the county getting carved up.

"It's worth it, because we have an opportunity to get Democratic representation, which has been missing from our county," Crawford said. "I've been here 15 years, and this is my first real opportunity to elect a Democrat."

Lincoln's downtown is flanked by fruit, vegetable and flower farms, as well as new subdivisions. The community and its neighboring suburbs have become a destination for people fleeing the San Francisco Bay Area's housing prices. That has helped change the once solidly conservative area into a political battleground where skilled mapmakers can draw winnable seats for Democrats.

Ed Church, a 61-year-old risk manager, was eating lunch at Simple Pleasures cafe in Lincoln when he contemplated Kiley's shift. A Democrat, Church has not been a Kiley fan and he was bemused by the congressman's move.

"If that's how he'd been initially and not so MAGA, I probably could have supported him," Church said of Kiley's independent status. Now Church, as a Lincoln resident, is in a purely Democratic district and will not have a say in Kiley's fate in November. His main criteria in the election will be "who's going to stand up to Trump?"

Across the street at a gun store, Wesley Johnson, 43, who considers himself a conservative independent, said he was dispirited by the state's redistricting.

"I feel Northern California is not represented fairly," Johnson said. "San Francisco, Sacramento and Los Angeles control everything."

He acknowledged Republicans were doing the same thing in states they controlled and said he did not know how it could stop.

"You're just cutting out the little people," Johnson said.

Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, the committee chairman who pressed for the contempt finding, said the constitutional protection did not apply because Democratic President Joe Biden had issued a preemptive pardon to Fauci, and he did not need to be concerned about potential prosecution.

Paul has long accused Fauci of misleading the public during the pandemic and the July hearing was the latest episode in his highly publicized confrontations with him. Paul has repeatedly called for Fauci to be prosecuted and imprisoned.

Johnson, chairman of the subcommittee on investigations, had sought to open a parallel avenue of congressional investigation about Fauci's role in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic, including the safety and efficacy of the COVID-19 vaccines.

title: Count Binface receives over a quarter of votes in Clacton by-election
description: The dustbin themed candidate got 9,455 votes and came second to Nigel Farage
fullText:
Count Binface, the self-styled intergalactic space warrior, has received nearly 10,000 votes in the Clacton by-election, his best performance yet.

The much-photographed election veteran was the main rival to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage in an election race caused by Farage resigning, only to run again - which sparked a mass boycott by the other main UK parties.

Farage has re-won his seat, receiving more than 22,000 votes in Clacton, on the Essex coast.

Binface received 26.9% of the vote while Farage won 63.3%. Binface had his highest share yet with 9,455 votes, having lost to no fewer than three prime ministers, and one who later became prime minister, in previous attempts.

But how many votes has he previously received? And where does he fit into the British tradition of spoofing politicians?

The man inside the bin is the comedian Jon Harvey, an Oxford graduate who has specialised in satire, writing scripts for BBC comedy shows The Thick of It and Have I Got News For You.

He first donned a bin on his head to stand for election in 2017, when he challenged the then Prime Minister Theresa May in her Maidenhead constituency, although back then he was known as Lord Buckethead, a character inspired by a Star Wars parody film.

He won 249 votes and viral fame, leading to an appearance on John Oliver's HBO show Last Week Tonight - as well as a legal dispute with another Lord Buckethead he described at the time as "an unpleasant battle on the planet Copyright".

Harvey found himself a different bin to cover his head and switched characters to Count Binface to take on the next Conservative leader, Boris Johnson, announcing himself as the leader of the Recyclons from planet Sigma IX.

He only won 69 votes, but was again able to take his place on stage as the election result was declared alongside a sitting prime minister, who was also flanked by a candidate dressed as the Sesame Street character Elmo, at his Uxbridge election count.

A third Conservative leader, Rishi Sunak, was in Count Binface's sights in the 2024 general election campaign.

He got 308 votes, which at the time was his best result.

The Monster Raving Loony Party's candidate, Sir Archibald Stanton, received 99 votes - 0.2% of the vote share.

In June this year, it was Andy Burnham's turn to face Binface in the by-election that paved the way for the then Greater Manchester Mayor to become prime minister.

Rather than studiously ignoring the intergalactic warlord, as some may have been tempted to do, Burnham shook him warmly by the hand as he was elected Labour MP for Makerfield.

Binface bagged just 95 votes to Burnham's 24,927.

While Nigel Farage won the Clacton by-election on Friday morning, Count Binface came second.

The Reform UK leader got 22,239 while Count Binface received 9,455. The intergalactic space warrior celebrated the number with his usual two peace sign fingers.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast after, Binface said: "I promised to be a local champion for Clacton and I thought to hear the verdict of the Clactonites was the least I could do."

The UK has a rich history of novelty candidates standing in elections, with Monster Raving Loony Party founder Screaming Lord Sutch - a rock musician who fought more than 40 elections in his trademark top hat and gold lame suit - first standing in a by-election in the 1960s. A different Lord Buckethead stood in 1987 and 1992, while comedian Al Murray's pub landlord stood against Farage in 2015.

Objections to such "frivolous" candidates date back even further - to 1918, when a £150 deposit was introduced for candidates. That was later upped to £500, in 1985, in large part due to the popularity of the Monster Raving Loony Party.

But the bar for entry remains fairly low: anyone over the age of 18 who can scrape together a £500 deposit and get support from 10 people in the form of signatures is allowed to stand as a candidate in UK elections.

That's why Count Binface has been able to stand in so many high-profile elections. He has, however, lost his £500 every time, after failing to meet the minimum 5% of votes cast in order for his deposit to be returned.

Yet Binface has had his moment in the spotlight each time.

That is because another British tradition means all election candidates must stand side-by-side on a stage at the election count to hear how many votes they have each received - it's a literal leveller, where everyone from prime minsters to a bloke dressed as a bin has the right to be seen and heard as an official candidate.

But all of these no-hope novelty candidates share a few serious aims: to poke fun at power, prick the pomposity of political elites, and allow people a protest vote.

title: Count Binface gets almost 10,000 votes in Clacton by-election
description: The self-styled intergalactic space warrior finished second to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
fullText:
Count Binface has enjoyed his best-ever election performance after receiving almost 10,000 votes and finishing second to Nigel Farage at the Clacton by-election.

The self-styled intergalactic space warrior said he was "1,000 times more popular" when standing against Farage compared to Andy Burnham, after he picked up 95 votes when challenging the now-prime minister in Makerfield in June.

Count Binface received 9,455 votes compared to Farage's 22,239. His 26.9% share of the vote is thought to be the highest ever for a novelty candidate.

He became the leading rival to Farage after the main UK parties boycotted the by-election triggered by the Reform UK leader, amid questions over his finances.

Farage had branded Count Binface the "candidate of the establishment" after claiming supporters of other parties had canvassed for him.

The contest in the Essex constituency saw a record 34 candidates for a Westminster Parliament election, although Farage did not attend the announcement of the result in person, denying Count Binface and others a chance to line-up alongside him in the Clacton Leisure Centre.

This led Count Binface to declare he was "the winning candidate in the room".

Reform UK said Essex Police had advised Farage not to attend the count "due to a credible threat against him".

The BBC has been told the force did not advise any candidate that they should not attend the count.

Count Binface is the satirical alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey, who has specialised in satire and been involved with BBC comedy shows, including The Thick of It and Have I Got News For You.

Harvey has previously stood in four parliamentary elections, including against prime ministers, and two London mayoral elections.

His previous best parliamentary result came in the Richmond and Northallerton vote against Rishi Sunak in the 2024 general election when he received 308 votes - 0.6% of the total share - and finished sixth out of 13 candidates.

The Clacton result was the first time that Count Binface has retained the £500 deposit candidates are required to make to validate their nomination.

It is repaid if a candidate polls more than 5% of the total number of valid votes cast in the constituency.

Nigel Farage returns as MP, winning Clacton by-election that major parties boycotted

Farage's by-election victory won't stop questions about finances

Farage had earlier told supporters at a Reform UK event that he was "damned if I'm going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory, a ringing endorsement of all that I've tried to fight for, and you've tried to fight for, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".

He then added he would not attend the count as Essex Police had told him about an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result".

Count Binface said he had asked police if was there "any credible threat of a disruption here", adding: "I can tell you they said unequivocally no, it was safe to go ahead."

He also told reporters that hearing the "verdict of the Clactonites was the least I could do".

He added: "All I will say to you is what happens next: let's all meet for part two of the Clacton by-election coming soon to a leisure centre near you."

This remark was a nod to a possible second by-election in Clacton, which could occur as a result of an investigation into Farage by Parliament's standards commissioner.

Farage resigned as an MP last month and stood in the subsequent by-election after facing intense scrutiny over financial support he has received.

The standards commissioner had been investigating Farage from May after the Reform leader did not declare a £5m gift he received from billionaire Reform donor Christopher Harborne before he became an MP.

Farage has argued he did not need to declare the gift, which he described as "unconditional".

The investigation was paused as a result of the by-election and resumed following his return to Parliament.

One possible outcome of a standards investigation is a suspension which triggers a recall petition. This process enables an MP to be removed and a by-election triggered if 10% of eligible registered voters sign a petition.

The other main UK parties are expected to put up a candidate if there is a second by-election.

Independent candidate Marc Wilkinson, who received 11 votes, was not happy with the attention Count Binface received during the campaign.

He said: "I was shocked that all the main parties didn't stand, I was shocked that Reform called the by-election, shocked that all the attention has been on Count Binface, most incredibly shocked by the extent to which the other candidates have been essentially ignored."

title: Infantino’s FIFA fate must go to an election, says Africa football chief
description: CAF have given under-fire Gianni Infantino their backing, and now say the FIFA president must stand in March’s election.
fullText:
Africa football confederation chief Patrice Motsepe says Gianni Infantino's future should only be decided by elections, after Ireland became the latest federation to withdraw its support for the embattled FIFA president.

Infantino is fighting to save his job after a barrage of criticism for his aborted plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

The governing bodies of European football (UEFA), North and Central America (CONCACAF) and Asia (AFC) stepped up the pressure on Infantino in a joint letter this week, declaring "trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority."

It is believed they want Infantino to resign before he has the chance to seek re-election in March next year.

But Motsepe, a FIFA vice president and Confederation of Africa Football (CAF) president, is adamant that Infantino's fate should be decided through the ballot box.

"If anybody has got any problem against anybody, whether it's Gianni, whether it is anybody else, follow the process, follow the FIFA process, simple as that," Motsepe told Sky News on Thursday.

"If you want to take him out, go for elections; let the 211 member associations decide. Do that and the vote will express whether they've got confidence in him or not.

"You've got to be very careful. There are elections taking place next year. Shouldn't we allow that process to continue?"

Motsepe was in Salzburg at the UEFA Super Cup on Wednesday to hold talks with UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin, whose organisation are threatening to boycott the World Cup and Club World Cup in protest at Infantino's scheme.

"I've heard so many stories about various issues and am careful to pass judgement on anything," Motsepe said.

"Everybody has a right to be heard. Let's have a hearing, and a proper forum."

CAF had already backed Infantino, and Motsepe claimed there was no breach of rules over the World Cup sell-off talks because the proposals would be submitted to FIFA members for final approval.

"There's a lot that's problematic and negative that they have to fix," Motsepe said.

"But he has apologised and said maybe there's a different way these things should have been done, but we also take advice."

However, there has been no end to the tidal wave of criticism engulfing Infantino.

On Thursday, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) became the latest FIFA member to withdraw its support for Infantino.

"Following an FAI Board Meeting, the decision was taken to rescind the letter of support that the Association supplied earlier this year," the organisation said.

"It has since written to FIFA to explain its reasoning. The Association is grateful for the support that FIFA provides to Irish football, but recent events have raised significant concerns regarding governance, transparency and the lack of meaningful consultation."

The English FA and Welsh FA had already withdrawn their backing for the 56-year-old Swiss.

Six Arab federations, including Qatar, Morocco and Egypt, offered their backing to Infantino on Thursday morning.

title: Trump-backed Mike Lindell refuses to concede Minnesota election loss
description: Mike Lindell, known as the "My Pillow Guy," said he wouldn't concede his primary loss until all the votes are counted. They're now all counted.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — Mike Lindell, a close ally of President Donald Trump known as the "My Pillow Guy," said he's not ready to concede in the Republican primary for Minnesota governor, and blamed potential voting irregularities despite losing by 11 percentage points to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth.

Even as it became clear he would fall short, the Trump-endorsed Lindell told reporters late Tuesday night that he believed 265,000 votes cast on Election Day hadn't been counted and could push him to the lead.

Asked on Aug. 11 whether he would concede if the Associated Press calls the race for his opponent, Lindell said he would not.

"The AP? Why would I listen to the AP?" Lindell said. "There's 265,000 votes left to count. I'm down by 18,000 now. We just gained 5,000. I'm not going to give up this race until the votes are counted. That's nonsense."

Lindell never pulled ahead, and the Associated Press called the election at 11:26 p.m.

More: Election results: Former MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell defeated in GOP primary

Lindell later told reporters he needed time to review the results, convinced the numbers didn't add up correctly based on the final batch of votes. He questioned Minnesota's computerized counting system, and said that all elections should be conducted by paper ballot.

"It just doesn't make sense, you guys. So we need a day. We're going to look into it," Lindell said, suggesting that there could have been voting irregularities, though not specifying what they were. "We've got different teams right now. I've been on the phone with three of them. And the one person said, 'Y, we've seen a couple of anomalies.'"

The Lindell campaign did not respond to an email from USA TODAY asking whether he's still refusing to concede his loss. Lindell has not made any additional public statements since his primary defeat.

More: Mike Lindell steps down as MyPillow CEO to focus on Minnesota campaign

Lindell, who stepped down as CEO of My Pillow to run for governor, has a history of denying election results and remains one of Trump's top defenders backing unfounded claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from Trump.

As Lindell watched a momentary shift in election returns going his way, he expressed confidence that he would overtake Demuth.

"If this is a sign, we will have the lead within an hour," Lindell said. "I mean, this is big news. This is a big jump. They must have started counting the day-of votes."

Lindell didn't get the bounce he needed, however, and Demuth secured the Republican nomination by double digits.

Final election phase begins in Pakistan-administered Kashmir despite banned group's boycott call
description: Voters went to the polls Monday in the final phase of elections for the legislative assembly in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, following weeks of violent protests and clashes with security forces that...
fullText:
MUZAFFARABAD, Pakistan (AP) — Voters went to the polls Monday in the final phase of elections for the legislative assembly in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, following weeks of violent protests and clashes with security forces that overshadowed campaigning in the disputed Himalayan region, officials said.

Men and women began lining up early at polling stations in Poonch district in the disputed Himalayan region, where four assembly seats were being contested.

Raja Shakeel, a spokesperson for the regional election commission, said voting was underway in four constituencies despite a boycott call by the outlawed Joint Awami Action Committee, or JAAC, which had urged residents not to participate in the election.

Pakistan's ruling Pakistan Muslim League-N party has already secured a majority and is expected to form the regional government for the first time in a decade after winning 24 of the 34 seats decided in the first two phases of voting.

Security was tightened around polling stations as voters cast ballots to choose their representatives in Kashmir, which is divided between Pakistan and India.

Both countries claim the Himalayan region in its entirety. They have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir since gaining independence from British colonial rule in 1947.

Several high-profile politicians are competing in the latest round of voting. Regional Prime Minister Faisal Rathore is seeking a seat from Haveli, while former Prime Ministers Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan, Sardar Tanveer Ilyas Khan and Mushtaq Minhas, a senior vice president of the PML-N, are also among the candidates.

Rana Sanaullah, a political affairs adviser to Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, predicted the PML-N would secure a two-thirds majority and form the next government in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

A PML-N victory would return the party to power in Pakistan-administered Kashmir after a decade.

Election officials say voting for seats yet to be decided is being conducted in phases because of security concerns and the electoral process is expected to be completed this month. Newly elected lawmakers will then be sworn in and choose the region's next prime minister.

The election campaign has been overshadowed by weeks of protests led by the JAAC, which has urged residents to boycott the vote. The regional government recently banned the group, citing security and public-order concerns.

The dispute between the JAAC and the regional government centers on 12 legislative seats reserved for people displaced from Indian-controlled Kashmir since the end of British colonial rule. The JAAC argues that the arrangement gives disproportionate political influence to people living outside Pakistan-administered Kashmir and has demanded the seats be abolished.

The seats were created to provide political representation to people displaced from Indian-controlled Kashmir who settled elsewhere in Pakistan because Pakistan-administered Kashmir lacked the capacity to accommodate them.

The JAAC, formed in 2023, has demanded greater political rights for people in Kashmir and the government says it accepted 36 of the group's 38 demands and maintains that the dispute over the reserved seats can be resolved only by the regional assembly.

title: GOP senators rally behind Thune in response to Trump jabs at leader
description: Senate Republicans are rallying behind Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) after President Trump declined to support the GOP leader serving another term following the midterm election. Many Rep...
fullText:
Senate Republicans are rallying behind Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) after President Trump declined to support the GOP leader serving another term following the midterm election.

Many Republican senators say Thune will have their full support, even if Trump backs a challenger, because of the Senate leader's refusal to abolish the filibuster to advance Trump's top legislative priorities, such as the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

"There's a lot of respect for John Thune. There's a lot of recognition of how he works and how difficult his job is and a belief that he's doing it really well under difficult circumstances," said Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).

Moran said Republican senators have been willing to yield to the president on a lot of issues but that they would draw a line against letting Trump push Thune out of his job or pick a replacement.

"I also think there are some things where the Senate seems willing to accede their privileges, but I think who our leader is, there's a real sense that that belongs to us," he said.

Even Senate conservatives who have ratcheted up pressure on Thune to keep the upper chamber in session during the August recess to debate the SAVE America Act acknowledge that Thune has had to navigate a political minefield as GOP leader.

"It's a hard job, it's really a hard job," said Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a leading proponent of the SAVE America Act.

Asked if he continues to have confidence in Thune despite the growing criticism from the White House, Scott noted that presidents often get frustrated with the Senate's 60-vote hurdle to passing their legislative priorities.

"I'm sure if I were president of the United States, I would be frustrated if everything I wanted didn't get done. So that's probably pretty common," the Florida senator said.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said he's doesn't "know of any movements to replace" Thune even though Trump has repeatedly expressed frustration over his agenda getting bogged down in the Senate.

"I think the president and John like each other. I think these are tough issues and they obviously disagree over things like the filibuster," Kennedy said.

Trump last week insisted in an interview with Punchbowl News that Republican voters are "not angry at me, but they are angry at Republicans" in Congress.

But even Trump's allies on Capitol Hill aren't buying that claim.

"I think Republicans are angry at all of us, I mean the voters. I think the voters are angry, period. And I think they're angry most about … cost of living, and I think that's what this election is going to be primarily about," Kennedy said.

"One of the reasons that the democratic socialists are winning elections is because they stand for something. Now what they stand for sucks, but a lot of their support is coming from young people who don't know history," the Louisiana senator continued.

GOP lawmakers think Trump has caused political headwinds for their party by not being more attuned to the affordability crisis, which Trump downplayed as a "hoax" issue driven by Democrats.

And while Trump has traveled around the country to talk about his economic accomplishments, he is prone to veering away from his script to hit on hot-button political issues, such as calls to pass the SAVE America Act to avert fraud in the upcoming election.

Thune has tried to shrug off Trump's criticisms in recent weeks, but they're becoming tougher to downplay as the president continues to suggest that the Senate GOP leader isn't getting his job done and that voters aren't happy with Republicans in Congress as a result.

Thune said he almost "expected" Trump to withhold his endorsement for him serving another term as Senate leader.

"That's probably to be expected," Thune said with a trace of resignation in his voice.

And Thune argued just as the Senate was leaving that his Republican colleagues have done a lot of heavy lifting to get the president's agenda passed, disputing Trump's accusations that they're not doing their jobs.

Thune said he and other Senate Republicans feel they are getting a lot done for Trump.

"I think we've had a really productive run. There are a couple things I said right from the very beginning are going to be difficult if not impossible — frankly more impossible — to do," he said of Trump's calls to pass the SAVE America Act and abolish the filibuster.

"That's the reality I have to deal with," Thune said of Democratic opposition to voting reforms and Republican opposition to lowering the threshold for passing legislation from 60 votes to a simple majority.

The GOP leader said the president is "entitled to his views," and Thune is "fine with that," but he argued getting Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed despite strong reservations from a handful of GOP senators, coupled with the prolonged absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), was a "good, solid win for the team and obviously … not an easy one."

"We'll keep grinding away and let the chips fall where they may," Thune added.

One Thune ally said Trump's public criticism of the Senate leader is a tactic he is using to put "pressure" on Thune to pass as much of the president's agenda as possible and predicted it could "change" after the election.

Even so, Trump's refusal to say whether Thune is "still the man for the job" — coupled with White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt's statement that Trump's "patience is running out" with Thune's job performance — has fueled the appearance that their personal relationship is on shaky ground.

Thune has winced or hinted at his frustration at times when asked about the latest rumble of dissatisfaction from Trump but has mainly stayed focused on enacting as much of his agenda as possible before Democrats have a chance to win back control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Yet a growing number of Senate Republicans see Trump and his low approval ratings — especially on the economy — as a bigger political problem than strategic decisions made by Thune and his leadership team.

GOP lawmakers are seeking to distance themselves from Trump ahead of the November election as polls show independent voters moving away from the president and Republican voters losing enthusiasm for him.

More than half the Senate GOP conference pushed back against the Justice Department's proposal to establish a nearly $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund for Trump's MAGA allies at a fiery meeting with Blanche in May.

GOP senators also quashed Trump's push for $1 billion in funding for the new 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom and are now currently resisting his call for immediate passage of a budget resolution to fund the unpopular military conflict with Iran.

A group of Senate Republicans last week bristled over the White House intervening in a stopgap spending bill to fund the government until Dec. 11 by adding language to delay the implementation of a ban on hemp-derived THC products — a policy rider that deeply divided their conference.

One GOP senator fumed the move was "not rational," given the uproar it created within the conference, to delay the implementation of the ban by only a month.

"I don't understand why this is an issue. What's the heartburn over just a few weeks? They say there's someone very close to the White House who has an interest in this," the lawmaker added, referring to media reports that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles's son-in-law, Bret Worley, is the CEO of companies that make hemp-derived intoxicating gummies and vapes.

GOP senators vented their complaints over the hemp-products rider to White House staff during a closed-door meeting but later acceded to the White House's will on the issue by voting early Saturday morning to table an amendment sponsored by Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) to strip the White House-backed hemp language from the government funding stopgap.

"This issue has got everybody in the conference spun up," the senator added. "If the president were to veto a CR [continuing resolution] over this? Wow. But that's kind of the worry."

title: What are your favourite new kits for the coming season?
description: BBC Sport has rounded up some of the best new kits released by clubs around the world over the summer - vote for your top 10
fullText:
As a new season draws near, football-hungry fans around the country will be tweaking their fantasy teams, making themselves experts on rumoured transfer targets and keeping eyes keenly trained on new kit releases.

It's an exciting time for collectors, whether they're looking for never-before-seen designs, classic shirts reimagined or niche releases from far-flung lands to impress their colleagues at five-a-side.

BBC Sport has rounded up a non-exhaustive list of some of the best kit releases for 2026-27 so far, ordered alphabetically.

Scroll down to the bottom of the page to vote for your top 10.

Marking 20 years since AC Milan's last Champions League title, the Rossoneri's new away shirt is modelled by legendary former player Filippo Inzaghi - who won the trophy twice with the club, including scoring a brace in the 2007 final in Athens to beat Liverpool - and current defender Davide Bartesaghi.

League One side AFC Wimbledon's away kit, in red and yellow, shares the same colour palette as the kit the team wore on the day of their promotion to the top flight for the first time ever on 3 May 1986.

Marking 20 years since the Gunners moved to Emirates Stadium, Arsenal's new home shirt has a bold red base, with white accents.

Mikel Arteta's men kick off their Premier League title defence against promoted side Coventry City on Friday 21 August.

The north London club have reprised their famous yellow for this season's third strip, with a kit reminiscent of away shirts worn by Arsenal players during the late 1980s.

Aston Villa's new home kit is an instant classic. However, the club were warned over sportswashing after revealing Visit Rwanda - the African country's tourist board - as their new front-of-shirt sponsor last month.

Atletico Madrid's new home shirt platforms the Rojiblancos' famous stripes, together with a subtle trident motif - a symbol associated with the club's fans, who gather at Madrid's Neptune Fountain to celebrate victories.

The Blaugrana have adapted their traditional stripes for this year's home kit. Hansi Flick will be aiming for a third successive La Liga title since taking over as manager in May 2024.

Adidas have gone for a retro revival with many of their kits this year and Bayern Munich's away strip sits very much in that vein - simple, clean and with the traditional trefoil logo. Vincent Kompany's team reached the Champions League final last season and have become one of the most exciting teams to watch in Europe.

Blackburn Rovers' new partnership with Umbro has been launched with an absolute stunner of a kit.

After they survived relegation from the Championship last season, manager Tony Mowbray returned to Ewood Park in June for his second spell in charge at the club.

Bournemouth struck a club-record deal with new kit supplier Hummel in May.

German manager Marco Rose will succeed Andoni Iraola at Vitality Stadium this season after the Spaniard departed having led the Cherries to their first ever European qualification.

In a commitment to affordability and sustainability, Brentford announced earlier this month that their new home kit would also be worn during the 2027-28 season.

Brighton's new home kit, with its subtle pinstripes and white neckline, draws heavily on the strip worn by the Seagulls during the 1983 FA Cup final, which they lost 4-0 in a replay against Ron Atkinson's Manchester United.

Celtic's new home shirt celebrates 60 years since the Lisbon Lions defeated Inter Milan to win the European Cup at the Estadio Nacional in Lisbon, with a commemorative badge and inscription inside the neck.

Chelsea's new home kit pays homage to their nineties 'Italian Renaissance', when Gianluca Vialli and Gianfranco Zola helped bring success to the club, including the 1997 FA Cup and 1998 League Cup.

Mexican side Club America's new home shirt is inspired by one worn during the 1998-99 season, with the club's crest blown up across the torso.

Manager Cesc Fabregas has turned Como into a serious outfit and this is a serious kit to match. The Italian side qualified for the Champions League for the first time last season and will be hoping to kick on from there.

Coventry City's new home shirt draws inspiration from the kit worn by players during the 1987 FA Cup final victory over Tottenham Hotspur.

The Sky Blues will return to the Premier League in August for the first time in 25 years after gaining promotion under manager Frank Lampard.

Scottish Championship side Dunfermline Athletic have released a shirt that harks back to the one they wore during the 1994-95 season.

The Toffees' new home shirt draws inspiration from marine flags found around the docks at the Hill Dickinson stadium.

Turkish club Fenerbahce's new away shirt is inspired by the first kit the club ever wore when they were founded in 1907.

Marking the club's centenary, Fiorentina's new home shirt features an embossed pattern inspired by the ornamental frames of Renaissance art found in the city of Florence.

Fulham's away shirt is a reinterpretation of an iconic chequered jersey worn 30 years ago during the 1996-97 season.

In 1996-97, Grimsby Town played in an away kit that was almost identical to one worn by the likes of Roberto Baggio, George Weah and Paolo Maldini at AC Milan. With Lotto returning as the League Two club's kit supplier this season, that design has been revived for a new generation of Mariners fans.

Launching their new partnership with Oxen, Hull City have released a very retro kit for the new campaign, evoking the shirts the Tigers wore during the late seventies.

Sergej Jakirovic's team will return to the Premier League for the first time in a decade this season, kicking off their campaign at home against Manchester United on Saturday 22 August.

Ipswich Town return to the Premier League this season after they were relegated at the end of the 2024-25 campaign.

The Tractor Boys' new home kit takes inspiration from the Sir Bobby Robson and Sir Alf Ramsey stands at Portman Road, with a motif copying the one that runs across the roof of the stadium.

After last season's experimental home kit, the Old Lady have returned to their traditional, thick stripes this year.

Leeds' new away shirt takes the Yorkshire rose from its club badge and repeats that motif across the base of the shirt. Blooming marvellous.

Liverpool's away shirt is inspired by the ticket stubs from European nights during the 1970s and 1980s. It also strongly brings to mind away and third kits worn during a successful period in the club's history during the late 1980s.

Liverpool's home kit for the 2026-27 campaign is a very conscious nod to the Adidas kit the Merseyside club wore between 1989-1991, during which time they won the 1989-90 First Division title under manager Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Lyon's home shirt for the new campaign pays tribute to the city, with Lyon's coat of arms silhouetted against the shirt sponsor and appearing as a subtle pattern across the stripes.

Manchester City's new home kit uses a sky blue gradient, with a print inside the neck, which reads, "Not Your Typical City". Following the departure of Pep Guardiola though, will it be typical City under new manager Enzo Maresca?

Manchester United's new away shirt is inspired by the Red Devils' 1988-90 third kit, which was only worn in three matches. The club have a history of success in blue however, having won both the 1968 European Cup final and 2017 Europa League final wearing blue kits.

Manchester United's new home kit, with its flat-knit striped collar and cuffs, is inspired by Red Devils kits from the late seventies.

To celebrate 150 years since they were founded, Championship club Middlesbrough have released this bold red and gold kit, with a special anniversary club badge displayed front and centre.

Napoli celebrate their founding in 1926 with this special kit in 'centenary blue', featuring a 100-year anniversary logo on the club badge.

Napoli's third kit evokes designs famously worn during the 1986-87 and 1988-90 seasons, when a certain Diego Maradona inspired the club to two Serie A titles.

Newcastle's new home kit uses what's been described as a 'disrupted stripe'. Just don't say it looks like a barcode. The Magpies are entering a new era this season after the shock departure of manager Eddie Howe.

French side Nice have released this classic home shirt and it is, dare we say, rather nice.

Nice's away shirt is another contender for kit of the season with its simple, but effective colour palette, classic fold-over collar and piping down the sleeves.

Nottingham Forest's home shirt is inspired by the mist that rolls in from the River Trent.

Oxford United teamed up with local street artist and lifelong U's supporter Andrew Manson to design this season's kit, along with a bespoke piece of artwork.

The European champions haven't tried to reinvent the wheel with this kit, but it oozes class. Can anyone stop Luis Enrique's side from winning a third successive Champions League trophy?

Primeira Liga champions Porto have released an away kit in gorgeous ruby - inspired by the port produced in the region as well as the River Douro.

Rangers' new home shirt is a classy affair. The Glasgow club will hope to exorcise the disappointment of last season's third-place finish under new manager Derek McInnes.

The stripes are narrower and there are interwoven diagonal lines, but this is still very definitely a Real Betis shirt - one of the most recognisable designs in European football.

Real Madrid have released their new away kit in a gorgeous, deep green, reminiscent of their 2012-13 third kit.

To celebrate their 100-year anniversary, La Liga club Real Oviedo have released a kit worth waiting a century for.

La Liga 2 side Real Valladolid's home shirt uses the club's traditional stripes, with a silhouette showing the Province of Valladolid stitched into the kit.

Sampdoria's home kit will remind fans of a certain vintage of Saturdays and Sundays spent watching David Platt represent the Serie A side on Channel 4's Football Italia.

To celebrate the club's 80-year anniversary, the shirt comes with a subtle anniversary logo embossed across the chest.

Sheffield United's away kit revives a classic style worn by the Blades during the 1975-76 season.

That campaign ended in relegation from the First Division for the Yorkshire club, but it's an iconic design nonetheless.

Ligue 1 side Strasbourg have joined the nineties revival. Their new away kit uses diamond graphics synonymous with Adidas kits from that decade, including the strips worn by the French side themselves between 1994-96.

In one of the more unexpected launches this summer, Sunderland have collaborated with the Elvis Presley estate to release this striking kit in a colourway synonymous with the King's early years in Louisiana.

Elvis' 'Can't Help Falling in Love' has been a matchday anthem for the North East club since the late seventies.

For their new home shirt, the Black Cats have drawn inspiration from the shirt worn by players during the club's first FA Cup victory at Wembley over Preston North End in 1937. A jacquard 'S' in the style of the handles of the FA Cup trophy is repeated across the base of the jersey.

After recording their highest ever WSL points total last season, Spurs are looking towards a bright future with big ambitions in the transfer market. Meanwhile, new manger Roberto de Zerbi is hoping to drag the men's side up from the depths.

To dare is to do and this kit is nothing if not daring.

Serie A club Venezia have released some of the most sought-after kits of recent years and this season's home shirt is sure to be no exception.

Wrexham's new home shirt pays tribute to their stadium, the Racecourse Ground, with a pattern reflecting the old Kop's barriers embossed into the weave of the fabric. The stand was demolished in 2023 to make way for redevelopment.

title: Thune, Trump, Senate conservatives reach deal to set aside budget, SAVE America Act impasse
description: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), President Trump and Senate conservatives reached a deal Friday night to set aside a vote on a budget resolution and defer action on much of the SAVE America...
fullText:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), President Trump and Senate conservatives reached a deal Friday night to set aside a vote on a budget resolution and defer action on much of the SAVE America Act until after the August recess, settling a fight that had divided Senate Republicans for weeks.

Conservative Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Rick Scott (R-Fla.) emerged from Thune's office in the Capitol after speaking with Trump and holding a two-hour conference meeting with GOP colleagues, and told reporters they had reached an agreement.

They said that there's now consensus within the conference to postpone action on a Senate budget resolution that would serve as a blueprint for a reconciliation bill until after the August recess and to vote immediately on a key element of the SAVE America Act — the requirement that voters show photo identification in federal elections.

Johnson, Lee and Scott, who have called on Senate GOP colleagues to cancel the August recess to debate and attempt to pass the full SAVE America Act, acknowledged they didn't have the votes to advance that bill anytime soon.

"We had about a two-hour conference meeting, trying to figure out what we need to do to come to an agreement to accomplish what the president wanted," Johnson said, acknowledging that the proposed budget resolution may have failed on the Senate floor because of a lack of enough Republican support.

"There was a concern whether or not it could actually pass, the budget resolution, tonight," he said, noting that some colleagues wanted substantially more funding for the Pentagon than the $73 billion proposed in a House-passed budget resolution. The budget resolution would serve as a blueprint for a party-line reconciliation bill Republicans aim to pass without needing Democratic support.

"There's certainly concern in terms of the need for our military. When the finest among us are in harm's way, is it really enough?" Johnson said. "The conclusion of the conference and then we had the discussion with the president, he agrees, don't take the vote tonight. Just work diligently through August and September to do an actually better budget reconciliation bill."

"We're all satisfied with that. So, we're not going to vote on budget resolution tonight and really work hard tonight," he said.

The conservative leaders say they're also "hopeful" on finding a way to vote soon on a continuing resolution to fund the government through Dec. 11 and to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general. Republicans had spent much of Friday searching for a deal to accelerate the timeframe for passing both priorities.

Lee indicated that he would not force Republican colleagues to vote on a politically sensitive adjournment resolution in order to embark on a five-week recess because he was satisfied with an emerging agreement to vote instead on a bill sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) to require voters to show photo identification in federal elections.

Lee said "of course" he's disappointed that the SAVE America Act won't pass anytime soon but acknowledged "we're not in a position right now where we have the wherewithal to pass it right now."

"But we are going to vote on a handful of things, including the Husted measure with photo ID, which is about half of what the SAVE America Act is," Lee said. "That will give us some indication of where we stand.

"Voter ID is a major component of SAVE America," he added.

Democrats defeated Husted's proposal to require voters to show voter identification in a 53-47 vote when he offered it as an amendment on Senate floor in March. The vote came during a lengthy debate on the SAVE America Act, which Senate Democrats have repeatedly blocked.

Democrats voted against Husted's amendment in March despite Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer's (N.Y.) claim that Democrats support photo ID requirements for elections.

Schumer told reporters in a March 15 press call that Democrats included a voter ID provision in their Freedom to Vote Act, which they introduced in 2021 when they controlled the Senate.

"Democrats support voter ID. In fact, we included it and it is included in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago. So, we're not opposed," Schumer said.

Lee said conservatives want to put Democrats on the record on the issue once again.

"We've got many Democrats who've said, 'I'm just fine with voter ID.'" Lee said. "We're going to find out where they are on that."

Johnson said Trump signed off on the plan to wrap up the Senate's work before the August recess.

"We're in total agreement. There's no argument about it," he said.

The Senate has already voted five times on the SAVE America Act or major elements of it but have failed to entice enough Democrats to overcome the 60-vote threshold for ending a filibuster.

Thune has repeatedly said that Senate Republicans don't have the votes to abolish the filibuster to pass election reform legislation, as Trump has demanded.

title: Fetterman says he'd win a Democratic primary today. What the polls say
description: U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., said he believed he would win in a Democratic primary if the vote were held today.
fullText:
While he can't run until 2028, U.S. Sen. John Fetterman believes that if a Democratic primary were held today, he would win.

During an Aug. 5 conversation in CNN's The Situation Room with Wolf Blitzer, Fetterman, D-Pennsylvania, responded positively to a question about how he might fare in a bid for reelection.

"Yeah," he said, then added, "I mean, I mean, that's — we don't know exactly, but overall, it's 2026, so it's, it's really kind of a theoretic."

The comment comes after questions have been raised by both Republicans and Democrats about whether or not Fetterman will switch parties, with Fetterman telling NBC News last month that he would no longer stay with the Democratic party if they "officially become the anti-Israel party."

A July poll from Quinnipiac University showed that 48% of Pennsylvania voters approved of Fetterman's performance in the U.S. Senate. He was up 77%–12% with Republicans, but down 69%–19% among Democrats and 48%–44% among independents.

The Quinnipiac poll also showed 52% of voters wanted him to leave the Democratic party, with just 31% saying they would like him to stay.

At the end of July, PennLive polled readers about whether or not they would vote for Fetterman if he were up for reelection this year. Of the 630 respondents, 58% said they would vote for someone else. 40% said they would probably (28%) or definitely (12%) vote for Fetterman.

As of Aug. 6, 2026, Fetterman had not announced official plans to run for reelection in 2028.

Fetterman ran as a Democrat in 2022, but there's been speculation that he'll switch parties, prompted by his votes in favor of President Donald Trump's cabinet picks, public criticism of Democrats and regular appearances on Fox News.

In April, Pennsylvania's GOP Chair Senator Greg Rothman said he was watching to see if Fetterman would jump ship, according to PennLive.

"We're still trying to wrestle with what happens if John Fetterman switched party and becomes a Republican," Rothman said.

Last month, Fetterman commented on the issue, telling NBC News that there was one condition that would cause him to leave his party.

"If they put that in our platform — no aid for Israel — and officially become the anti-Israel party, then yeah, that's a red line for me," Fetterman said. "Democrats, we always should support Israel. That's our special ally, you know? In the only democracy in the entire region, that's Israel. So I'm always proud to stand with Israel."

Fetterman was only one of two Democratic senators to confirm at least 50% of Trump's cabinet nominees in 2025, voting in favor of 12 of 23 candidates, according to Ballotpedia. Still, he remains an ideological Democrat based on GovTrack's Ideology-Leadership Chart, which shows several Democratic senators who are ideologically closer to the Republican party.

Fetterman scored the majority of votes in Allegheny County on Election Night 2022, recording 363,873 votes (63.4%) while Republican challenger Dr. Mehmet Oz received 200,672 (34.9%), according to Commonwealth of Pennsylvania election results.

The votes from the Pittsburgh area and Allegheny County made up more than 13.2% of Fetterman's 2,751,012 total votes in 2022.

Finch Walker is the Pittsburgh Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network. Contact Walker at FWalker@usatodayco.com. Instagram: @finchwalker_. X: @_finchwalker.
